candidate.answerReason: At their first simultaneous return to A, the boys have completed 5 and 9 laps. Their combined 14 laps produce 14 meetings after the start, including the finish.

methods.label: Lap counts and opposite motion
methods.explanation:
Because the boys run for the same amount of time, their distances, and hence their lap counts, are in the ratio \(5:9\). To meet at \(A\), both must have completed whole numbers of laps. Since \(5:9\) is already in lowest terms, the first positive whole-number pair of lap counts is \(5\) and \(9\).

For opposite directions, their positions agree exactly when their combined traveled distance is a whole number of track circumferences. Their combined distance increases continuously, so each successive whole circumference produces exactly one meeting. By the finish, their combined distance is \(5+9=14\) circumferences. Thus the meetings after the start correspond to combined distances of \(1,2,\ldots,14\) circumferences. The fourteenth is the finish, leaving \(\boxed{13}\) meetings, choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses speed-distance-time relationships, a reduced ratio, and elementary counting of whole laps.

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is counting opposite-direction meetings on a circular track. Distance ratios and integer multiples locate the first joint return. This method does not require an LCM calculation.

review.mathematicalCheck: The first simultaneous return has lap counts 5 and 9 because their ratio is reduced. Meetings occur exactly at whole circumferences of combined travel. The combined total reaches 14 circumferences, so excluding both endpoints leaves 13 meetings.
